sm: Author Nate describes growing up in the wheat fields of Northern Idaho and wanting kids to feel that their own ordinary world is magical, since we live on a ball of lava circling a star. That desire is the root of his Ashtown Burials series. The hosts welcome him and the illustrator Forest to a Thanksgiving-week episode. Nate says the series began when a Wodehouse-style aunt at Random House asked what he most wanted to write, and he chose a secret order of explorers that could pull history and myth from around the globe into one story. His original editor returned for book four, and the first book dates to about 2007. The host admits he has not read the books, so a spoiler warning is given.

The hosts name Antigone Smith and Diana Boone as favorite characters, praising strong female characters who are not girl bosses. Nate explains that the secret is placing them beside strong men, since both come from families of strong men and feel secure in their strength. One host sums up the setup as a Reformation story: a secret explorers society, the Order of Brendan, is corrupt within while pagan enemies press from outside. Nate adds that Brendan the Navigator founded the order in the 500s. He sailed to the Great Lakes to bury undying dark creatures and relics, and that is where Ashtown was founded.

Nate says he set the series in Wisconsin after a book tour where bored kids insisted their lives were dull. Ashtown is a maximum-security prison built by Brendan, and the Order that guards it has decayed. Cyrus and Antigone Smith are offered membership, then despised and pushed into the worst basement. Nate says this mirrors Christian kids in the West who inherit a legacy others scorn. A host says reading the series to your kids is one practical thing parents can do. Nate calls the books true to how institutions age, rather than allegory, with managers who dislike the heirs of the original vision, and he compares them to the stewards of Gondor.

Nate points out hidden details, such as an approved 1946 English oath whose Latin original has the gospel stripped out, and says Antigone is named for the Greek figure known for family loyalty. Asked why he is so hard on characters he likes, he compares them to barley that suffers and makes the best whiskey. He says stories should be a rib eye, not morphine, and contrasts Cyrus with Harry Potter, who is only a victim. Cyrus is modeled on Cyrus the Great and Old Testament heroes who were pushed until they became heroes. Asked for the toughest ordeal, he says he hit eleven and cannot go higher.

In book four, Nate says, Cyrus must deal with the angel of death and gets foreknowledge of his choices, so he must decide whom to save and what to risk. The main conflict is between the Order and transmortals, old enemies who broke their treaties, plus apostates inside the Order such as Dr. Phoenix. Characters come from across history, including Gilgamesh, John Smith, Radu Bey, and a giant turtle named for Ponce de Leon. Nate says the unifying question is how death is rightly defeated. He contrasts a pagan pursuit of immortality at others' expense with sacrificial fearlessness, and links the pagan side to modern transhumanists.

The hosts ask how Nate chose which transmortals side with the good guys. Arachne is a victim of Minerva, and Nolan Calis, a starving boy who stole Gilgamesh's fruit, is cursed to shed like a snake. Those who grasped immortality by theft and blood are enemies, while victims are open to the Order. Nate explains the clay Golems of book three, meant to judge justly but who find everyone wanting. He also describes the Ordo Draconis, which wants to open every burial, and the fiery Irish monk Niffi, a noble sectarian you want in the fight but not in command. Rupert Greaves is his Prester John figure, a steward like Aragorn meeting Faramir.

Nate says Rupert Greaves becomes the natural leader of the remnant because he stays faithful to the mission. The hosts compare the Order to a National Geographic Society with more money and supernatural powers. Nate says he wanted kids to learn achievable things like fencing, combat, Latin and flying a plane, not spells, and has heard from kids who trained themselves. Forest then discusses the covers. He worked to keep them exciting without being too specific or scary, and the final style is a woodcut that Mark cut by hand on linoleum. He also made painted end pages, favors book one's dragonflies, and Nate favors the fourth cover with its giant nautilus.

Asked how the Order wins, Nate says he chose middle grade fiction for its concrete resolutions and happy endings. Light wins and the remnant triumphs, but it is a temporary victory short of the final judgment. The Order is reborn and reinvigorated, yet faces a huge rebuilding task amid rubble. He hopes readers become better characters and says he loves when people discover that a character or detail was real. For readers who want to go further, he recommends Herodotus, Josephus, the Old Testament, the Iliad, the Odyssey, the Aeneid and Beowulf, and mentions a book called The Lost Cities of Africa. He also notes that the books had a mismatched early run and the fourth went unpublished for years.
